0.title: Biblical Principles for Every Relationship
0.essay:
Think back over the last week. A short word at breakfast. A colleague you cannot quite warm to. A neighbour you have nodded to for six years and never named. A friend you keep meaning to ring. Someone at church you avoid, for no reason you could defend. Most of the joy in our lives comes to us through people, and so does most of the ache.

Made for one another

In a world that was still without sin, God looked at the man he had made and said, “It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Adam had God, a garden and good work, and it was still not good. We were made by a God who has always been Father, Son and Holy Spirit, living in love before there was a world. Made in his image, we are made for relationship.

So when Jesus was asked for the greatest commandment, he gave two that cannot be pulled apart: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment. And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:37–39).

Why it is hard

Sin has bent us in on ourselves. We need people too much, or we keep them at arm’s length. We use them, fear them and misread them, and they do the same to us.

Where we are going

This study does not offer techniques for being liked. It offers the gospel, which changes what we bring to every relationship: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). It gives general principles for relating to people of every kind: family, friends, colleagues, neighbours, church members and strangers. Particular ground is covered in other studies, which this one points to rather than repeats: Friendship & Hospitality, Christian Marriage, Christian Parenting, Leadership, Handling Conflict, Forgiveness & Reconciliation and Dealing with Difficult People.

The chapters

Seeing People Rightly; The Heart You Bring; Words and Ears; Everyday Love; Boundaries, Differences and Trust; and In the Moment and Afterwards.

For reflection

Which of your relationships gives you most joy at present, and which most ache? What would you most like to be different about the way you relate to people?

1.title: Seeing People Rightly
1.essay:
Before we say a word to anyone, we have already decided what they are. Useful. Interesting. In the way. A threat. Not worth noticing. We rarely think it in words, but we act on it. How we treat people follows from how we see them, so that is where Scripture begins.

An image-bearer

“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). This is said of human beings and of nothing else in creation. It is true of the person at the till, the toddler screaming on the bus, the man asleep in a shop doorway and the woman with dementia who no longer knows your name. Their dignity was not earned by being clever or useful, and it is not lost by being weak, awkward or old.

James draws the practical conclusion. He is appalled that with the same tongue we bless God and “curse people who are made in the likeness of God” (James 3:9). To despise a person is to slight the one whose likeness they bear. C. S. Lewis once observed that we have never spoken to a mere mortal: every person we meet will live for ever. Nobody is ordinary.

A sinner

The Bible is equally plain about a second thing: “for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Every person you know is bent, as you are. This is not a gloomy thought. It is a freeing one. It means you need not be shocked when people let you down, and they need not be shocked when you do. No friend, husband, wife, child or pastor can carry the weight of being your saviour. Expecting less of people in that sense lets you be more patient with them, and more grateful.

A sufferer

And a third thing. When Jesus looked at a crowd, “he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36). Everyone you meet is carrying something you cannot see. “The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy” (Proverbs 14:10). The colleague who snapped may have been awake all night with a sick child. The friend who has gone quiet may be frightened about a hospital letter. This does not excuse sin, but it makes us slow to judge.

We need all three together. See only the image of God, and we become naive. See only the sinner, and we become cynical. See only the sufferer, and we excuse everything. Jesus saw people whole, and so he could be tender and truthful with the same person in the same conversation.

Honour

From this comes a short and sweeping command: “Honor everyone” (1 Peter 2:17). Not only the impressive. Everyone. And within the church Paul turns it into a kind of contest: “Outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans 12:10). It is the one competition in which everybody is trying to give the prize away.

Honour is mostly shown in small things. Looking at the person who is speaking to you. Learning a name and using it. Turning up when you said you would. Not talking over someone. Thanking the person whose work usually goes unnoticed. Speaking of people when they are absent as you would if they were in the room.

No favourites

James pictures a church meeting. A man with a gold ring and fine clothes walks in, and so does a poor man in shabby clothes. One is shown to a good seat. The other is told to stand, or to sit on the floor. James does not call this bad manners. He calls it sin: “My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory” (James 2:1). And again, “if you show partiality, you are committing sin” (James 2:9).

We do it without thinking. We brighten for the confident, the attractive, the well connected and the people like us. We look over the shoulder of the shy, the poor, the very old and the socially awkward. But “the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

The gospel removes the ground of favouritism. None of us was welcomed by God because we were impressive. We came with nothing in our hands, and the Lord of glory received us. So Paul can say, “From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh” (2 Corinthians 5:16). The cross has changed the way we value people. Each brother or sister in the church is, in Paul’s words, “the one for whom Christ died” (Romans 14:15). You cannot rank someone low whom Christ loved at such a cost.

An example

A regional sales manager in his fifties is warm with clients and attentive to directors. For four years he has walked past the woman who cleans his office each evening without once learning her name. One Sunday his minister preaches on James 2, and it stings. The next evening he stops, introduces himself and asks her name. Over the following weeks he learns that she works two jobs and has a son sitting his exams. Nothing dramatic follows. He simply greets her by name now, and asks about the exams. He is ashamed that it took four years, and glad that it did not take five.

For reflection

Whom do you tend not to notice? Which of the three, image-bearer, sinner or sufferer, do you most easily forget about other people? Who naturally gets your best attention, and who gets what is left? What is one small way you could show honour this week to someone who rarely receives it?

2.title: The Heart You Bring
2.essay:
Two people can do the same kind thing for opposite reasons. One gives a neighbour a lift because he cares about her. Another does it because he cannot bear to be thought unhelpful. From outside they look the same. Relationships go wrong at the root long before anything shows in the fruit.

Needing people and loving people

We can come to others with empty hands or with full ones. If I come needing you to do something for my heart, I cannot love you freely. I am a customer, and you are my supplier. The need may wear several disguises, and most of them look like love.

Approval. I am kind so that you will like me, and I cannot disagree with you in case you stop. Control. I help you so that things will be done my way, or so that you will owe me. Comfort. I stay close while you are easy company, and drift away when you become costly. Being needed. I rescue people because I do not know who I am unless someone depends on me.

There are simple tests. What happens in me when I am not thanked? When you say no to me? When you manage well without my help? If the answer is resentment, I was not only giving. I was trading. The study The Fear of Man looks closely at the hunger for approval that lies under much of this.

Loved first

Scripture does not tell us to try harder to be unselfish. It tells us where love comes from. “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another” (1 John 4:10–11). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger at sin. Christ bore what we deserved, so that nothing now stands between the believer and the Father’s welcome.

The order matters. First we are loved. Then we love. If the welcome of God is settled, I no longer have to get acceptance out of you. You stop being my supply and become my neighbour. I can enjoy you without clutching you. I can serve without being noticed, hear your no without collapsing, and tell you something hard because I am no longer afraid of losing you. Paul puts both halves in one sentence: “welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God” (Romans 15:7).

Counting others more significant

“Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others” (Philippians 2:3–4).

This does not mean pretending to be worthless, or believing that others are worth more to God than you are. It means that their interests carry real weight in my decisions. The question I carry into a room changes. It is no longer “How am I doing?” but “How are they?” Humility is not thinking badly of yourself. It is being free to stop thinking about yourself for a while.

Paul does not leave this as advice. He shows us a person. “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:5–7). Then lower still: “he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8).

Here is the wonder of it. There was one person who truly was more significant than everyone else in the room, in every room he ever entered. And he counted us. The eternal Son looked to our interests, not his own comfort, all the way down to a cross. When we are asked to put others first, we are being asked to live inside a love that has already put us first.

Humbled and confident at once

The gospel says two things to us together. We are more sinful than we like to admit, so we can never look down on anyone. And we are more loved than we dared to hope, so we need not look up at anyone in fear. That combination is rare. Most of us swing between feeling superior and feeling small. The gospel makes a person humble without cringing and confident without swagger.

We see it in Jesus on the night before he died. “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist” (John 13:3–4). He knew who he was, and so he could kneel. People who are secure do not need to guard their dignity. They are free to serve.

An example

A woman in her forties is the person her church relies on: rotas, meals, lifts, the lot. She is also exhausted, and quietly bitter that nobody seems to see it. One Sunday someone else is thanked from the front for a job she had mostly done, and she drives home furious. The strength of her anger frightens her. Slowly she sees that much of her serving has been a payment for being indispensable. She does not stop serving. She lays down two of her jobs, does the rest more quietly, and begins to pray before each one, “Father, I already have your smile.” The bitterness does not vanish overnight, but it thins.

For reflection

Which do you most want from people: approval, control, comfort, or to be needed? How do you react when you are not thanked, or when someone says no to you? What would change in one particular relationship if you came to it already full of the love of Christ? Read Philippians 2:5–8 slowly. What does it stir in you?

3.title: Words and Ears
3.essay:
Most relationships are built or broken in conversation. And most of us assume that the skill lies in what we say. Scripture begins somewhere else. It begins with our ears.

Quick to hear

“Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger” (James 1:19). Most of us are quick to speak and slow to hear. Proverbs is blunt about it: “If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13). And again, “A fool takes no pleasure in understanding, but only in expressing his opinion” (Proverbs 18:2).

Listening is a way of loving. Attention is one of the most valuable things we have, and to give it is to give something of ourselves. We know the marks of poor listening because we have been on the receiving end. The other person is preparing a reply while we are still talking. They turn our story into theirs: “That reminds me of when I …” They offer a solution before we have finished describing the problem. They glance at a phone.

Good listening is patient. “The purpose in a man’s heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out” (Proverbs 20:5). Deep water takes time to draw. It needs a question, then a pause, then another question. Often people do not need our answer nearly as much as they need to be heard.

We listen like this because we have been listened to. “I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice and my pleas for mercy. Because he inclined his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live” (Psalm 116:1–2). The Maker of heaven and earth bends down to hear his children. We can surely bend towards one another.

Truthful

“Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another” (Ephesians 4:25). Paul’s reason is striking. A body in which the eye deceives the hand cannot work. Falsehood is wider than plain lies. It includes flattery, exaggeration, the convenient half-truth, and the yes that really means no.

Yet truth is to be spoken in a certain way: “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). Truth without love bruises people. Love without truth flatters them and leaves them where they are. The first is often pride, and the second is often fear. We need both together, as they were together in Christ.

Gracious

“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). That verse gives three questions to ask before speaking. Will this build up? Does it fit this moment and this person? Will it give grace? A true remark at the wrong time, or in front of the wrong people, can do real harm.

Paul says the same about our talk with those outside the church: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Colossians 4:6). Each person. There is no one way of speaking that suits everybody. Love pays attention to who is in front of it.

Encouraging

“Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing” (1 Thessalonians 5:11). Most people hear a great deal more correction than encouragement. The best encouragement is specific and true. Not “You’re wonderful”, but “I noticed how patiently you spoke to her, and it helped me.” When you see the grace of God at work in someone, tell them. They often cannot see it themselves. “Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body” (Proverbs 16:24).

Trustworthy

“Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered” (Proverbs 11:13). When someone tells you their story, you are holding something that belongs to them. It is not yours to pass on, not even dressed up as a request for prayer. Few things build a relationship like the discovery that what you said stayed where you put it, and few things end one as fast as finding that it did not.

There is one important limit. If someone tells you that they or another person are in danger, or that a child is being harmed, you must not promise to keep it secret. Love then means telling the people who can protect them.

The study The Tongue deals fully with gossip, harsh words and the other sins of speech, and with how the tongue is tamed. It is worth reading alongside this chapter.

An example

A retired teacher, a widower, is known in his street as the man people talk to. He is not especially clever with advice, and gives little. He asks a question, then another, and next time he remembers the answers. A young neighbour who had just been made redundant said months later that their ten minutes over the fence were the only minutes in his week when he did not feel like a problem to be solved.

For reflection

In conversation, are you more often listening or waiting to speak? Who in your life needs to be heard rather than advised? Is there a truth you have been avoiding saying, or one you said without love? Whom could you encourage this week, and what exactly would you say?

4.title: Everyday Love
4.essay:
Love in the Bible is seldom grand. Mostly it is ordinary: a meal, some patience, a promise kept, a visit. The New Testament does not ask many of us to die for one another. It asks all of us to put up with one another on a Tuesday.

One another

Again and again the apostles use the same two words. “Love one another with brotherly affection” (Romans 12:10). “Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality” (Romans 12:13). “Live in harmony with one another” (Romans 12:16). “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). “Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32).

These commands are given first to the church family, but the same love then spills over to everyone: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18).

Notice how Paul introduces such a list in Colossians. “Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience” (Colossians 3:12). Before he tells us what to put on, he tells us who we are: chosen, holy, loved. The clothes are for people who already belong to the family. We are not kind in order to become beloved. We are kind because we are.

Bearing with

Paul goes on: “bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive” (Colossians 3:13). Bearing with and forgiving are two different things. Forgiving is for sins. Bearing with is for everything else: the loud laugh, the slow driving, the story told for the third time, the different way of loading a dishwasher. A large share of the friction in homes, offices and churches is not sin at all. It is simply other people being other people.

It helps to remember that somebody is bearing with you. Your habits are as odd to others as theirs are to you. For real wrongs, and what to do about them, see the study Forgiveness & Reconciliation.

Rejoicing and weeping

“Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). To weep with someone you do not need clever words. You need to turn up, sit down and stay. To rejoice with someone is often harder, especially when they have received the very thing you wanted. The study Envy & Comparison is about that.

The golden rule

“So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 7:12). Jesus puts it positively. He does not only forbid doing to others what we would hate. He tells us to do for them what we would want. That takes imagination. What would I want if I were the new person in this room? If I were the one who was ill, or grieving, or the youngest in the office, or the only one who did not understand the joke?

And Jesus presses it past the people who can pay us back. “If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them” (Luke 6:32). The mark of his people is kindness that expects no return, because that is how the Father treats us: “he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil” (Luke 6:35).

Keeping your word

Psalm 15 asks who may dwell with God, and part of the answer is the person “who swears to his own hurt and does not change” (Psalm 15:4). He keeps a promise even when it has become costly. Proverbs observes how rare that is: “Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find?” (Proverbs 20:6).

Reliability is love in its slow form. It means arriving when you said you would, answering the message, returning what you borrowed, finishing what you offered to do. Warm feelings are easy to announce. Trust is built by small promises kept over years. It is better to promise less and do it.

Generosity, thanks and small courtesies

Paul remembered a saying of the Lord Jesus: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). Generosity is not only about money. It is time, attention, a meal, a lift, the benefit of the doubt. “Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:18). The study Friendship & Hospitality says much more about opening our homes.

Gratitude matters too. When Jesus healed ten men with leprosy, one came back to thank him, and Jesus asked, “Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine?” (Luke 17:17). He noticed. People who are thanked know that they have been seen.

And Scripture even has a word for manners. We are “to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people” (Titus 3:2). Please and thank you, a door held, a prompt reply, letting someone finish a sentence. Paul immediately gives the reason, and it is the gospel. We ourselves were once foolish and hard to live with, “But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (Titus 3:4–5). God has shown great kindness to people who did not deserve it. Small courtesies are one of the ways that kindness passes on.

An example

A student nurse moves to a city where she knows no one. An older couple at church invite her to Sunday lunch. The food is plain. They keep going: a message before her exam, a lift when her car fails, a question about her mother’s operation, remembered weeks later. Three years on she says she cannot recall a single sermon from those first months, but she remembers whose table she sat at. She is now the one who looks for the new face on a Sunday.

For reflection

Whose habits do you find hard to bear with, and who may be bearing with yours? Is there a promise, large or small, that you have not yet kept? Apply the golden rule to one person you will see tomorrow: what would you want in their place? Whom have you never properly thanked?

5.title: Boundaries, Differences and Trust
5.essay:
If love meant saying yes to everyone, trusting everyone and agreeing with everyone, then Jesus did not love. He disappointed crowds, kept his own counsel and disagreed openly. Yet no one has ever loved as he did. Love is wiser, and stronger, than niceness.

Love is not pleasing everyone

Early one morning Jesus went out alone to pray. His disciples tracked him down with what sounded like good news: “Everyone is looking for you” (Mark 1:37). He replied: “Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out” (Mark 1:38). He left real needs unmet in Capernaum, because he knew what his Father had sent him to do.

We are not the Saviour, and we have far less to give than he had. Every yes is a no to something else, often to the people closest to us. A kind, plain no is not unloving. Jesus said, “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). The study Busy, Tired & Restless says more about living gladly within our limits.

Paul gives a helpful pair of sentences. “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2), and, three verses later, “each will have to bear his own load” (Galatians 6:5). A burden is something too heavy to carry alone, and love gets underneath it. A load is a person’s own daily responsibility, and love does not take it from them. Doing for people what they ought to do for themselves is not always kindness. Sometimes it is our own need to be needed.

One caution. The language of boundaries can become a cover for selfishness. The question is never simply “What suits me?” It is “What does love for God and for this person require of me?”

Love for all, trust with wisdom

Love is owed to everyone. Trust is not. When crowds in Jerusalem believed because of the signs, “Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man” (John 2:24–25). He loved them, and would die for sinners like them. But he did not put himself in their hands.

Trust is given in measure, as a person proves faithful. “The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps” (Proverbs 14:15). It is wise to be warm with all and to confide your deepest things to a proven few. It is also wise to choose close companions with care, since they shape us: “Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm” (Proverbs 13:20). “Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare” (Proverbs 22:24–25). And when trust has been broken, forgiveness may be given at once, while trust is rebuilt slowly.

Disagreeing well

The church in Rome was divided over food and special days. Paul names the temptation on each side: “Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him” (Romans 14:3). The freer person is tempted to sneer, the stricter to condemn. Paul asks both, “Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another?” (Romans 14:4).

Our list is different: schooling, alcohol, politics, how to spend Sunday afternoon, how to bring up children. On the gospel and on the plain commands of Scripture we stand firm. But that list is shorter than the list of our opinions. On the rest we can say “I see it differently” and remain friends. “So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding” (Romans 14:19).

Different by design and by background

Some people think aloud, and others need a day before they can answer. Some plan, and some improvise. In one culture a direct no is honest. In another it is rude, and a refusal comes wrapped in courtesy. Many quarrels start when we read a difference as a fault. It is usually better to ask than to assume: “When you went quiet, what was going on for you?”

With those who do not believe

“Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time” (Colossians 4:5). Unbelieving friends, relatives and colleagues are not projects. They are people to be honoured, listened to and enjoyed. We are to be honest about our hope, “always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). Jesus was called a friend of sinners. He drew near to them without joining in their sin. The study Evangelism takes this further.

When it is not safe

None of this means enduring abuse. Violence, threats, sexual coercion, control of your money or movements, and constant degrading are not “difficulties” to be borne in the name of love, submission or forgiveness. Your safety, and the safety of any children, comes first. Get to a safe place and tell someone you trust. If you are in danger, call the police or the emergency services. Harm to a child must be reported to the authorities. A faithful church will help you do this, and will never ask you to keep it quiet.

For people who are persistently hard to deal with, such as the critical, the controlling or the manipulative, see the study Dealing with Difficult People.

An example

A man in his thirties has never been able to say no. Not to his brother, who borrows money and does not repay it, nor to his manager’s weekend requests, nor to any committee. His wife and children get what is left of him. An elder at his church asks him one question: “When you say yes to everyone, who are you saying no to?” He tells his brother, kindly, that there will be no more loans, though he will gladly sit down and help him plan a budget. His brother is cool towards him for a month. Then, slowly, things thaw.

For reflection

Where do you say yes out of fear rather than love? Is there someone you are carrying who needs to bear their own load, or someone with a real burden whom you have left alone? Have you trusted too quickly, or held back trust from someone who has earned it? With whom do you disagree, and how could you honour them while still disagreeing?

6.title: In the Moment and Afterwards
6.essay:
Principles need hands and feet. This last chapter gathers some small habits that anyone can begin this week. They are not rules for earning love. They are ordinary ways of giving away the love we have been given.

Names and stories

The Lord says to his people, “I have called you by name, you are mine” (Isaiah 43:1). The good shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3). To be known by name is to be treated as a person. So learn names, and write them down if that helps. Then remember the story that goes with the name: the interview on Thursday, the daughter abroad, the scan results. Next time, ask.

Good questions

Some questions close a conversation, and some open it. “How are you?” usually gets “Fine.” Try “How has this week really been?” or “What are you looking forward to?” or “How is your mother now?” Then ask one more question about the answer before you say anything about yourself.

Being present

Put the phone away, face down or in a pocket. The person in front of you is the one God has given you for these few minutes. Jesus was once hurrying through a crowd to the bedside of a dying girl when a woman touched his cloak. He stopped. He “looked around to see who had done it” (Mark 5:32), heard her whole story, and called her “Daughter”. He was never too busy for the one in front of him.

Apologising quickly

When you have been sharp, late, careless or unkind, say so soon and say it plainly: “I was wrong to speak to you like that. I’m sorry. Will you forgive me?” Leave out “but” and “if”. People who know they are forgiven by God can afford to be wrong in front of others. When a disagreement has grown into something larger, see the study Handling Conflict.

Thanking and praying

Paul began letter after letter in the same way: “I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy” (Philippians 1:3–4). It is hard to stay cold towards someone you pray for by name. Then tell them. A two-line message, “I thanked God for you this morning”, may be the kindest thing they read all week.

The first step towards someone you have neglected

Most of us have a friend we have not rung for two years, or a relative we have let drift. “Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it” (Proverbs 3:27). Do not wait until you can explain yourself. Send something short and honest: “I’ve been a poor friend, and I’m sorry. I would love to hear how you are.” They may not reply. Paul’s words are realistic: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18). Your part is the first step.

If you are lonely

Some who read a study on relationships feel mainly an ache, because there are so few people in their lives. Loneliness is not a sin, and often it is nobody’s fault. Bereavement, a move, illness, singleness or caring for someone at home can empty a life of company. The Lord Jesus knew it. In Gethsemane his friends slept, and then “they all left him and fled” (Mark 14:50). Paul knew it as well: “At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me. May it not be charged against them! But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:16–17).

God’s ordinary answer to loneliness is his people: “God settles the solitary in a home” (Psalm 68:6). So where can you start? Start small and keep going. Go to the same small gathering every week, since friendship grows from being seen repeatedly. Join a team that does something. Talking side by side over a task is often easier than face to face over coffee. Look for someone who seems more alone than you are, and ask them a question. And tell a pastor or an older Christian how things are.

If loneliness has settled into lasting low mood or despair, please see a doctor. That is wisdom and no failure of faith, and the study Depression & the Christian may help. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust.

The friend of sinners

His enemies gave Jesus a nickname and meant it as an insult: “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Luke 7:34). It is our whole hope. On the night before he died he said, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). And then, to men who within hours would run away and leave him: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends” (John 15:15).

He did not choose his friends for what they could give him. He knew the worst about them, and he stayed. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). The one who knows you completely has called you his friend, and paid for the friendship with his life.

That is what we bring to every other relationship. We do not come as beggars hoping that someone will at last make us feel accepted. We come as people already befriended by the Son of God, with something to give.

An example

A man in his sixties, recently widowed, used to slip out of church during the last hymn. One week he decides on a single change. He will stay for coffee and learn one name each Sunday. He writes them in the back of his Bible. A year later he is one of those who welcome people at the door. He still goes home to a quiet house, and some evenings are very hard. But on Sundays people know his name, and he knows theirs.

Further reading

Timothy Lane and Paul David Tripp’s Relationships: A Mess Worth Making is a readable book on this whole subject. Timothy Keller’s short book The Freedom of Self-Forgetfulness shows how the gospel frees us from ourselves so that we can attend to others.

For reflection

Which one habit from this chapter will you begin this week? Is there someone you have neglected to whom you could send a short message today? If you are lonely, what is one small, repeatable step you could take? What does it mean to you that Jesus calls you his friend, knowing all that he knows?
